title: An Educated Guess: Deriving Statistically Aligned Gradient Estimates for Zeroth-Order Optimization
claim: Informed perturbation directions align far better with the true gradient than random ones, and the gap grows with structure and probe count.
layout: 4 panels in a row, grouped in pairs, shared legend below
description: Four scatter plots in one row share a bottom legend. The left pair is titled 'Fashion-MNIST MLP, Hidden layer'. The right pair is titled 'CIFAR-10 CNN, Conv layer 4'. Within each pair, the left panel shows per-batch credit and the right shows per-sample credit. The x-axis is the number of probes, on a log scale from 1 to 4096 (1024 for the CNN). The y-axis is the angle in degrees between the estimated and true gradient. Colored dots with error bars show five methods: NP in red, WP/SZO-0 in dark blue, NTWP in orange, SZO-1 in light blue and SZO-∞ in green. Angles start near 90° and fall as probes increase. WP stays near 90° in the batch panels. NP stays high on the convolutional layer. SZO-1, SZO-∞ and NTWP fall fastest, reaching about 40° or lower. In the per-sample MLP panel, NP and SZO overlap.
caption: The angles between estimated gradients computed by NP, WP, SZO-κ and NTWP against the true backpropagation gradient for randomly initialised layers in MLP and Convolutional Networks. For each network, the left panel uses per-batch loss-difference credit and the right panel per-sample credit; points show the mean angle over 20 randomly seeded initialisations (batch of 128) against the number of probes n, with error bars of ±1 standard deviation. Left pair, the gradient alignment angle is shown for the first layer of our Fashion-MNIST MLP network. Under per-sample credit these angles clearly show the equivalence of NP and SZO-κ on a linear layer, as theorised in this work. Right pair, the gradient alignment angle is shown for the last 3 × 3 convolutional layer (64 →64 channels) of our CIFAR-10 CNN model. On convolutional layers NP suffers significantly from its lack of shared perturbation across kernel positions. Note, these angles were measured by perturbing only the layer in question and leaving all other network layers unperturbed.
abstract: As novel hardware architectures are explored for the purposes of machine learning, including neuromorphic chips, asynchronous systems, and ASICs, effective learning algorithms are highly desirable. While backpropagation is the standard for differentiation on standard hardware, its requirement for global synchrony and exact differentiability limits the exploration of exotic algorithms on non-traditional substrates and devices. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimisation methods, such as SPSA and weight perturbation, offer a compelling alternative by estimating gradients through inference-only passes; however, these methods have historically suffered due to the `curse of dimensionality', where random perturbations become increasingly misaligned with the true gradient in high-dimensional spaces. In this work, we move beyond blind random noise by deriving zeroth-order search directions from activation geometry available during the forward pass. This leads to a family of Spectral Zeroth-Order methods, SZO-$Îº$, whose directions solve local response-based gradient-guessing objectives under explicit stochastic assumptions. These methods explore feature-supported directions that are more likely to produce informative loss responses. Using multilayer and convolutional networks, we analyse gradient alignment, bias-variance structure, and training stability of these methods relative to standard perturbation baselines and backpropagation.
